tex_content.html:
\begin{example} \end{example}[Adjoint Representations of Lie Groups] 1. chC:C.10

  1. If $G$ is an abelian Lie group, then $C_\varphi $ is the identity map for every $\varphi \in G$, so the adjoint representation is trivial: $\text{Ad}(\varphi ) = \text{Id}_\mathfrak {g}$ for all $\varphi \in G$.

  2. Suppose $G$ is a Lie subgroup of $\text{GL}(n,\mathbb {R})$. Then for each $A \in G$, the conjugation map $C_A(B) = ABA^{-1}$ is the restriction to $G$ of a linear map from the space $\text{M}(n,\mathbb {R})$ of $n \times n$ matrices to itself. Its differential, therefore, is given by the same formula: $\text{Ad}(A)X = AXA^{-1}$ for every $A \in G$ and $X \in \text{Lie}(G) \subseteq \mathfrak {gl}(n,\mathbb {R})$.

\end{example}

There is also an adjoint representation for Lie algebras. If $\mathfrak {q}$ is any Lie algebra, a representation of $\mathfrak {q}$ is a Lie algebra homomorphism from $\mathfrak {q}$ to $\mathfrak {gl}(V)$, the Lie algebra of all linear endomorphisms of some vector space $V$. For each $X \in \mathfrak {g}$, define a map $\text{ad}(X): \mathfrak {g} \to \mathfrak {g}$ by $\text{ad}(X)Y = [X, Y]$. This defines ad as a map from $\mathfrak {g}(\mathfrak {g})$, and a straightforward computation shows that it is a representation of $\mathfrak {g}$, called the adjoint representation of $\mathfrak {g}$.

The next proposition shows how the two adjoint representations are related.
